'''Gladys Louise Palmer''' (1895 – June 27, 1967) was an American [[Social statistics|social statistician]] who "gained worldwide attention for her research on manpower problems and labor mobility" and for her work on the standardization of labor statistics.{{r|amstat}}

==Education and career==
Palmer earned a bachelor's degree from [[Barnard College]] in 1917, studied for a master's degree at [[Bryn Mawr College]] from 1917 to 1918, as Carola Woerishoffer Scholar in Social Economy and Social Research,{{r|bmgrad}} and completed a Ph.D. in 1924 at the [[University of Pennsylvania]].{{r|amstat}}

She became an instructor in [[economics]] at [[Vassar College]]{{r|amstat|vascat}} and [[Hollins University|Hollins College]], and then moved to the Industrial Research Unit of the [[Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania]] in 1931. By 1953 she was Research Professor of Industry and director of the Industrial Research Unit at the Wharton School. Beginning in the 1930s, she was also a frequent consultant for various federal agencies in Washington DC.{{r|amstat}}

==Books==
Palmer's books include:{{r|amstat}}
*''Union Tactics and Economic Change: A Case Study of Three Philadelphia Textile Unions'' (de Gruyter, 1932){{r|utec}}
*''I am a Woman Worker: A Scrapbook of Autobiographies'' (edited with Andria Taylor Hourwich, Affiliated Schools for Workers, 1936)
*''Labor Mobility In Six Cities: A Report On The Survey Of Patterns And Factors In Labor Mobility, 1940-1950'' (Social Science Research Council, 1954){{r|lm6c}}
*''Philadelphia Workers in a Changing Economy'' (de Gruyter, 1956){{r|pwce}}
*''The Reluctant Job Changer: Studies in Work Attachments and Aspirations'' (with Herbert S. Parnes, Richard C. Wilcock, Mary W. Herman, and Carol P. Brainerd, de Gruyter, 1962){{r|rjc}}

==Awards and honors==
In 1946, Palmer was elected as a [[Fellow of the American Statistical Association]].{{r|fasa}}
